paragraphs:
(Hyman describes him as a great preacher in the fourth generation in Eretz Israel.)
Apparently he received from R' Abba bar Kahana, as in Tanchuma Tazria 8, where he spoke in his name. His precious homilies reached Babylonia as well, as cited at the end of Berakhot, where he said: Anyone who pushes the hour, the hour pushes him; from here, the owner of the beam should take hold of its thick part. Anyone who enjoys a meal in which a Torah scholar is present is as though he enjoys the radiance of the Divine Presence. One who takes leave of his fellow should say to him 'Go to peace'; of the dead, 'Go in peace.'

In the midrashim he is called R' Avin the Levite, berabbi (ברבי). In Tanchuma Vayera 46 he tells, in figurative language, how Satan came to incite Abraham and Isaac. There, Chayei Sarah 2 and Vayishlach 21, he expounds the verse: What is 'talpiyot' (Song 4:4)? That all mouths pray toward it. There, Vaera 14, he says that Israel became rich from the plague of blood, because the Egyptian paid Israel full silver to give him water. There, Naso 34, he said: What is 'the King of Glory'? That He apportions of His glory to those who fear Him. He is likewise mentioned in Tanchuma Shemot 1 and 7, Bo 40, Beshalach 13, Tetzaveh 4, Ki Tisa 4, Tazria 4, Emor 20, Bechukotai 6, and Hyman quotes Bamidbar Rabbah ch. 14:3: 'R' Avin the Levite son of R' Yosef said.' Hyman suggests that it was written בר"י, meaning 'ברבי', and from this was made 'bar Yosef'.

notes.text: Rashi on Berakhot64a explains the beam idiom through Jacob’s responsibility for the children he raised: the one responsible should take hold of the matter and seek mercy.

Hyman proposes that בר״י, understood as berabbi, was misread as bar Yosef. The precise role of berabbi and the reported father-name variant remain unresolved; no unknown father called Rabbi is supplied.
